channel.title: Ajahn Funn Ācāro Quotes
channel.description: Dhamma quotes by Ajahn Funn Ācāro, updated every 24 hours

item.title: Ajahn Funn: See? Sitting here, your mind is still suffering — heavy, sluggish, drowsy, dull, miserable. It torments body and self, pain here, ache there.…
item.description:
Kamma Arises from Body, Speech, and Heart – Mental Kamma Is the Inclining of Mind

See? Sitting here, your mind is still suffering — heavy, sluggish, drowsy, dull, miserable. It torments body and self, pain here, ache there. It gives rise to diseases, dangers, defilements, nuisances, evil and depravity, misery and hardship. This is vipassanā. We know clearly and see truly. The truths (sacca-dhamma) do not come from elsewhere. Quickly recollect Buddho to cut it off. Do not leave it. If we leave it, we will continue to be poor, suffering people, continue to be evil and depraved. We don't want these things, do we? So see: when the mind is not good, that is suffering. Contemplate until it is certain. This is what we call kamma — that or this. Where does kamma come from? Kamma does not come from the sky, air, trees, mountains, or hills. Kamma by body (kāya-kamma), kamma by speech (vacī-kamma), kamma by mind (mano-kamma) — kamma arises from our body, from our speech, from our heart.

So kamma arises from this. At this moment, our bodily kamma is already good, our verbal kamma is already gone. Only mental kamma remains — the inclining of mind. Whatever kamma we incline toward, whether good kamma or bad kamma. Kammassako mhi — I am the owner of my kamma.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore, let us all strive to practice meditation, to focus and look, to determine and observe. You don't need to find something elsewhere…
item.description:
Observing What Is Yours: Everything Is Already Within Yourself

Therefore, let us all strive to practice meditation, to focus and look, to determine and observe. You don't need to find something elsewhere to observe. Observe what is yours. You already have everything within yourself. Emptiness is already there. Non-emptiness is already there. Happiness is already there. Suffering is already there. Everything is here right now. Observe what you have. However it is established, keep watching it just like that. Watch to know. And do not grasp this or that as a self, as a soul. The matter is simply that. We must all understand this point. That is why we come to do kammaṭṭhāna – kamma means action, what we do; ṭhāna means foundation, place. Establish it to abide. If it is empty, know it. If it is not empty, know it. To abandon, we must contemplate the basic kammaṭṭhāna. The teacher taught the basic kammaṭṭhāna so that we would know according to reality. He taught about hair so that we would know what hair is like. Is it a person? Is it something? Is this hair clean or unclean? This is the method to remove our lust, greed, hatred, and delusion, to remove our craving concerning self-identity.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: “Physical phenomena” means our body. We should come and take a good look at it. Why? We want to look into this body…
item.description:
Come and Look at This Body We Hold Onto as Our Self

“Physical phenomena” means our body. We should come and take a good look at it. Why? We want to look into this body that we hold onto as our self—a “being,” an “individual,” a “man,” or a “woman”—so as to contemplate it. We depend on it, we claim it as our self, and so he wants us to look at it. Why? So that we’re not deluded by it. He wants us to know this physical phenomenon so that we can abandon our pride, abandon our passion, aversion, and delusion, ignorance, craving, clinging, becomings, and births. If we don’t come and look at it, we’ll hold onto it as our self. But exactly where is it our self? Come and look.

When the Buddha taught the Five Brethren, he taught them the Discourse on Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion. In that discourse, he said, Idaṁ kho pana bhikkhave dukkhaṁ ariya-saccaṁ: “Monks, what is the truth of suffering? These four truths.” He told them to become acquainted with these truths: Jātipi dukkhā: Birth is suffering. We don’t come to suffering from anything else. We suffer because of birth. So contemplate it. The Buddha taught the religion so that we can know this. We’ve already been born, so why do we still suffer? We suffer because of birth.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ – Dhamma protects the one who lives by Dhamma. Beings depend on Dhamma; Dhamma depends on beings. If beings…
item.description:
Dhamma Protects Those Who Live by Dhamma

Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ – Dhamma protects the one who lives by Dhamma. Beings depend on Dhamma; Dhamma depends on beings. If beings practice Dhamma well, Dhamma brings goodness to us. If we practice well, conduct ourselves well, Dhamma brings virtues and goodness, brings happiness and prosperity. If we practice badly, do bad deeds, Dhamma brings bad things in the present and the future. This merit and wholesomeness that we have made is called paṭipattipūjā – the supreme, most excellent offering. From now on, let us sit every day, come to the monastery every day, practice every day. I have explained it. Wherever there is an obstacle, wherever it is not good, we must correct it there. Some people say the mind is not staying – where does it go that it is not staying? Actually, the mind has been staying since birth. The idea that the mind is not staying comes from delusion due to ignorance (avijjā). It is deluded. We must sit and look at this "not staying" – where is it creating becoming? Bhave bhavā sambhavanti – it goes around creating small and large states of becoming. We must sit and look: is that becoming wholesome or unwholesome? Wholesome is happiness, ease, coolness of heart. Bad becoming: our mind is not good, suffering, troubled, agitated, leading to a bad destination (duggati) in the present and the future.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Try to find a way out—so what if it kills you? What’s wrong with finding a way out? What are you still attached…
item.description:
Try to Die Outside of the Noose: Don’t Tie Yourself Down

Try to find a way out—so what if it kills you? What’s wrong with finding a way out? What are you still attached to? What are you still infatuated with? Try to be more resolute! We come into this world alone and we go alone. So who is it that dies? What leads us back to birth? Be done with it! Develop your goodness. That’s better than dying in a heap of suffering. Better than dying in worries—dying in the noose. Try to die outside of the noose. That’s what’s really good. Don’t tie yourself down.

It all comes from the mind, fabricating the idea that “This is mine, that’s mine, this property’s mine, this money, these possessions are mine, this clothing is mine, these homes are mine, these children and grandchildren are mine”: nothing but “me” and “mine.”

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Why do we look closely? In order to abandon clinging to the aggregates (upādānakkhandha), to abandon personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), to abandon skeptical doubt…
item.description:
Abandoning Personality View by Seeing the Truth of Hair, Nails, Teeth, Skin

Why do we look closely? In order to abandon clinging to the aggregates (upādānakkhandha), to abandon personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), to abandon skeptical doubt (vicikicchā), to abandon attachment to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa) – not anything far away. We bring it in, we contemplate the primary meditation subject (mūla-kammaṭṭhāna). When we ordained, the teacher taught this mūla-kammaṭṭhāna. We think that a kammaṭṭhāna monk is one who lives in the forest, but no – everything is kammaṭṭhāna. The mūla-kammaṭṭhāna teaches: kesā – hair. Whose hair? Where is it? Wherever the hair is, right there is the kammaṭṭhāna. Lomā – body hair – the kammaṭṭhāna of body hair. Nakhā – nails – the kammaṭṭhāna of nails. Where is it? Dantā – teeth – the kammaṭṭhāna of teeth. Where is it? Taco – skin – the kammaṭṭhāna of skin. Where is it? It envelops our whole body. These five things – this is the kammaṭṭhāna. Why did the Buddha teach the mūla-kammaṭṭhāna? Because these are the root cause that deludes beings in this world. Seeing hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, they mistake them for a self, for a being, for a person – “me” and “him,” “beautiful” and “handsome.” When we see them like that, we become deluded.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? When the mind is in the sensual plane, it roams among…
item.description:
Transcending the Sensual Plane: Contemplating the Body to Generate Disenchantment

What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? When the mind is in the sensual plane, it roams among forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, and mental phenomena (dhammārammaṇa) – that is its object. It is called one who delights in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, contacts, and various mental objects. This is called the mind abiding in the sensual-sphere realm (kāmāvacara bhūmi), in the existence called the sensual realm (kāmabhava).

What is it like for the mind to transcend the sensual plane? It lets go of external forms, external sounds, external smells, external tastes, and the many contacts and mental objects. It sees only this individual body of ours. It contemplates this conditioned body of ours, fixed right on itself, not sending the mind elsewhere or far away. It sees only our own conditioned body – its deterioration, its decay, or sees the conditioned body exactly as it is: with hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin. There is nothing else beyond this, nothing superior to this. Whether happiness or suffering, seeing deterioration and decay, or seeing breaking apart, the mind then abandons this form. Nibbidā arises – disenchantment with this form. Because this form has no core, no substance, no essence.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: The Buddha established the religion in the Tipiṭaka, in the Abhidhamma – He did not establish it elsewhere. Some of us say we…
item.description:
The Five Aggregates Are Established for Us to Know and See

The Buddha established the religion in the Tipiṭaka, in the Abhidhamma – He did not establish it elsewhere. Some of us say we have not studied the conventions (paññatti). We should come to know the conventions.

He established the Dhamma and Vinaya, saying: Cha paññattiyo – khandhapaññatti, āyatanapaññatti, dhātupaññatti, indriyapaññatti, puggalapaññatti. He established the religion in this way. He laid them down for us to come to know and understand. Khandhapaññatti – He established the five khandhas. I have explained this before: He established rūpa (form), vedanā (feeling), saññā (perception), saṅkhārā (mental fabrications), viññāṇa (consciousness). Let us look into it: Where is rūpa? It is this sitting here – that is called the rūpakkhandha. Why did He establish the khandhas? So that we would know these things, how they exist. Are they happiness or suffering? Are they good or bad? As for the vedanākkhandha – painful feeling, pleasant feeling, neutral feeling – let us examine. This is exactly what He established. The saññākkhandha – recognition, labeling, memory of this and that – He established it here. The saṅkhārakkhandha – formation, composition. Look: right now, are we fabricating wholesome or unwholesome states? We should know, we should see. It is not that the sky or air fabricates wholesome or unwholesome states – how would we know that?

item.title: Ajahn Funn: That we can live like this is due to the puñña (merit), vāsanā (latent tendencies), and pāramī (perfections) we have built up over…
item.description:
Dāna-Pāramī: Giving Up Much, Letting Go Much, Gains Great Reward

That we can live like this is due to the puñña (merit), vāsanā (latent tendencies), and pāramī (perfections) we have built up over many lives and many births.

And puñña and kusala (wholesome deeds) are nothing far away – they are precisely dāna-pāramī (perfection of generosity), sīla-pāramī (perfection of morality), and bhāvanā-pāramī (perfection of meditation).

We already know dāna: giving up, abandoning, letting go. Whoever gives up much, lets go much, gains great ānisaṃsa (reward). Whoever gives up little, lets go little, has little ānisaṃsa. Macchariya – stinginess, possessiveness – that is greed. We must give it up and become a generous donor. That is, we give away those very possessions, wealth, and objects – nothing else. It means to nurture oneself, just as the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha, before attaining magga and phala (path and fruition), built up his perfections, including this dāna-pāramī. Understand this: dāna is our provision. When we have done enough of it, we need not fear traveling a long distance. It is like coming to this monastery here. If we haven't prepared anything, we have nothing. But if we have prepared, we need not fear hunger or hardship, fear suffering or difficulty.
